method: Scripture is primary for biblical statements; original inscriptions are primary for their own imperial claims and surviving exemplars. This archive does not presume that shared events establish every biblical detail or that a later royal claim proves a command chronology. All case interpretations await qualified independent expert review; neither source coordinates nor automated tests constitute that review.
chronology_note: Stages are teaching-order groupings, not mutually exclusive exact-year boundaries. Samaria's capture and imperial consolidation are debated and may involve multiple episodes. Apparent exact royal totals may vary between exemplars.

stages.title: Before the siege
stages.focus: Tribute, northern conquests and a new vassal king

stages.title: The siege
stages.focus: Hoshea, Shalmaneser V and biblical regnal synchronisms

stages.title: Sargon's accounts
stages.focus: Competing royal attribution, deportation numbers and preserved text variants

stages.title: Provincial aftermath
stages.focus: Resettlement, administration and limited surviving witnesses

cases.heading: Menahem and the first documented tribute
cases.object: British Museum 118899 + 118900, Nimrud inscribed wall slabs
cases.royal: The edited royal tribute list includes Menahem of Samaria among rulers who made payment to Tiglath-pileser III. This is a tribute witness, not a siege or conquest account.
cases.scripture: Second Kings 15:19-20 names Pul of Assyria, relates Menahem's payment, and describes raising silver from wealthy Israelites.
cases.meeting: Menahem and Assyrian tribute are part of the same historical setting. The Assyrian ruler Tiglath-pileser III is conventionally identified with biblical Pul.
cases.limits: The surviving Assyrian list does not independently establish every monetary figure, collection method, or political motive given in Kings. The inscription does not describe the later siege of Samaria.
cases.uncertainty: The list is a royal retrospective and its lines partly overlap other compositions; document both copy and edited reading.

cases.heading: Northern losses and the geography of deportation
cases.object: Nimrud royal summary inscription reconstructed from damaged copies
cases.royal: The edited inscription discusses Bīt-Ḫumrî (the Assyrian designation for Israel), people taken to Assyria and losses to the kingdom before Samaria's final fall.
cases.scripture: Second Kings 15:29 records northern territories taken and inhabitants deported by Tiglath-pileser. First Chronicles 5:26 recalls the exile of eastern Israelite tribes.
cases.meeting: Both records discuss Assyrian encroachment and removal of people before the final Samaria crisis.
cases.limits: Neither witness supplies a complete household-by-household census. The earlier northern deportations must not be conflated with Sargon II's later claims about Samaria.
cases.uncertainty: The Q003455 inscription is broken; identifying precisely which people and areas occur in each fragment depends on specialist restoration.

cases.heading: Pekah, Hoshea and the broken succession line
cases.object: Nimrud royal summary inscription reconstructed from damaged copies
cases.royal: The edition names Pekah, king of Israel, and says Tiglath-pileser installed Hoshea. The verb concerning Pekah's death is damaged and may allow 'I killed' or 'they killed'.
cases.scripture: Second Kings 15:30 attributes the conspiracy against Pekah and his killing to Hoshea, who then succeeds him.
cases.meeting: Both sources know of Pekah's removal and Hoshea's accession, though they assign emphasis differently.
cases.limits: The broken Assyrian verb cannot independently prove whether the Assyrian ruler, Hoshea, or others killed Pekah. Avoid converting a restoration into an undisputed historical fact.
cases.uncertainty: The RINAP editor explicitly flags alternative restorations and disputed readings of the damaged signs in Q003455 line 17'.

cases.heading: Shalmaneser V and the three-year siege
cases.object: Specialist reign synthesis - not a surviving siege inscription
cases.royal: Contemporary official royal inscriptions surviving from Shalmaneser V's brief reign are scarce. The Assyrian Empire Builders chronology reconstructs his western campaigns and considers the formation of Samaria as a province; it does not provide an extant Assyrian siege annal from him.
cases.scripture: Second Kings 17:3-6 names Shalmaneser and describes Hoshea's subjection, imprisonment and the siege; 18:9-10 synchronises a three-year siege with the reigns of Hoshea and Hezekiah.
cases.meeting: The reign of Shalmaneser V is the critical setting for the named biblical siege; scholarly reconstruction associates him with the end of Israelite independence.
cases.limits: This comparison uses secondary specialist synthesis, not an invented Shalmaneser V inscription. The final city's capture and whether further action followed under Sargon II remain disputed.
cases.uncertainty: The absolute years and sequence of campaign, siege, capture and formal provincial reorganisation are reconstructed from limited and uneven witnesses.

cases.heading: Sargon II's claim to the capture of Samaria
cases.object: Khorsabad (Dur-Sharrukin) royal display inscription, several exemplars
cases.royal: Sargon's later palace inscription claims he surrounded and captured Samaria, removed inhabitants, conscripted chariots, and imposed a governor and tribute. It is a first-person imperial claim, not a neutral timestamp of siege events.
cases.scripture: Second Kings 17:5-6 and 18:9-11 recount the siege, fall and deportations while explicitly naming Shalmaneser at the beginning of the campaign.
cases.meeting: Samaria's capture, deportation and Assyrian power appear in both traditions.
cases.limits: Shalmaneser's named siege and Sargon's later personal conquest claim need not be silently identified as one attested command action. Some scholars argue one campaign, others multiple actions or later royal appropriation.
cases.uncertainty: The edition's annal and display composition traditions assign episodes differently; its own commentary notes the chronology is not straightforward.

cases.heading: 27,290 is a royal figure with variant readings
cases.object: Khorsabad display inscription with variant copies
cases.royal: The main edited exemplar reports 27,290 people taken from Samaria. The edition's apparatus also identifies readings of 27,280 and apparently 24,280 in other exemplars; the figure varies between witnesses.
cases.scripture: Second Kings 17:6 reports that Israelites were taken into Assyria and names settlement locations, without giving the number 27,290.
cases.meeting: Population removal is a shared theme, but the numerical precision belongs to Assyrian royal rhetoric and its surviving exemplars.
cases.limits: 27,290 cannot be presented as an independently verified modern population census or as a number supplied by 2 Kings. The other edited figures must not be hidden.
cases.uncertainty: The damaged signs, exemplar variants, what was counted, and the royal purpose of the tally still require critical historical assessment.

cases.year: Recounted in later Sargonic prism text
cases.heading: A second Sargon inscription has a different count
cases.object: Nimrud prism, incomplete and restored in places
cases.royal: The Nimrud Prism also discusses Samaria's rebellion, seizure, chariots, resettlement and imperial administration. Its population figure is damaged and is represented differently from the main Khorsabad display edition; the edition notes a proposed 47,280 reading.
cases.scripture: Kings records deportation following Samaria's fall, without the Assyrian palace figures or their copy differences.
cases.meeting: Sargonic records offer more than one Assyrian textual witness to claims of Samaria's takeover and resettlement.
cases.limits: A different manuscript is not automatic independent corroboration of a number when texts belong to the same royal propaganda system. Variant counts must not be averaged or converted into false certainty.
cases.uncertainty: The Nirud Prism reading and restorations are specialist editorial questions; neither the exact number nor the reign-specific assignment is settled simply by comparing English summaries.

cases.year: Assyrian provincial aftermath, late eighth century BCE
cases.heading: Resettlement and the reshaping of Samaria
cases.object: Khorsabad royal annals, damaged signs and restoration commentary
cases.royal: The restored annal text presents the takeover of Samaria, deportations, resettlement and installation of a governor. Large portions are supplied by scholarly restoration with parallel royal texts.
cases.scripture: Second Kings 17:24 describes settlers relocated into Samaria from named places, while 17:6 records the exile of Israelites to locations in the Assyrian sphere.
cases.meeting: Both narratives describe population movement and an altered political and demographic landscape.
cases.limits: The annal's restored text cannot directly identify every person or place in the biblical account. Biblical and royal language each selects details for different purposes.
cases.uncertainty: Sign restoration, translation, dating and the proposed sequence of one or more stages of transfer require independent review.
